steps.tx: A **sickle cell anaemia** represents the prototypic hereditary hemoglobinopathy, transmitted as an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a single point mutation in the beta-globin gene on chromosome 11p15. The mutation involves a single adenine-to-thymine (GAG to GTG) base transversion at codon six, resulting in the substitution of non-polar valine for negatively charged glutamic acid, producing abnormal hemoglobin S.
steps.say: Sickle cell anaemia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a single point mutation on chromosome eleven. A single base swap at codon six replaces hydrophilic glutamic acid with hydrophobic valine, creating haemoglobin S. This subtle chemical change fundamentally alters how haemoglobin behaves when oxygen levels drop.

steps.tx: The central molecular pathomechanism is the **polymerization of deoxygenated HbS**. Upon deoxygenation, the exposed hydrophobic valine residues create a sticky patch on the beta-globin chain that binds complementary docking sites on adjacent tetramers. HbS molecules aggregate into long, insoluble helical filaments termed tactoids. These rigid polymers distort the flexible biconcave erythrocyte into an elongated, rigid crescent shape.
steps.say: When deoxygenated, the mutant valine acts like a sticky patch, locking adjacent hemoglobin S molecules together into long, rigid crystal rods called tactoids. These insoluble polymers distort the red blood cell from a pliable disc into a stiff, pointed crescent sickle cell.

vis.title: Molecular and Biophysical Dynamics
rows: Shifts HbS into deoxygenated polymer state
Protects infants during first 6 months of life

steps.tx: Repeated cycles of sickling and unsickling inflict severe cumulative damage on the erythrocyte membrane skeleton. Calcium influx activates Gardos channels, expelling potassium and water, transforming cells into dehydrated, dense, **irreversibly sickled cells**. These rigid drepanocytes are incapable of deforming through narrow splenic sinusoidal slits, triggering chronic extravascular hemolysis by splenic macrophages, shortening red cell lifespan to ten to twenty days.
steps.say: With each round of sickling, the red cell membrane is battered. Intracellular calcium rushes in, driving out potassium and water. The cell becomes a dense, dehydrated, irreversibly sickled cell. These rigid cells cannot squeeze through splenic sinusoids and are demolished by macrophages, slashing red cell lifespan from one hundred twenty days down to just two weeks.

right.title: Irreversible Sickle Cells
points: Dehydrated with high MCHC and low potassium
Destroyed rapidly in splenic red pulp

steps.tx: Repeated microvascular infarctions within the splenic red pulp lead inexorably to **autosplenectomy** by early childhood. Successive episodes of sickling, thrombosis, and ischemic necrosis replace splenic lymphoid tissue with dense fibrous scar tissue and calcified iron-calcium deposits known as Gandy-Gamna bodies. Functional asplenia leaves patients immunologically vulnerable to overwhelming encapsulated bacterial infections, particularly Streptococcus pneumoniae and Salmonella osteomyelitis.
steps.say: Repeated sickle blockages in the spleen cause progressive infarction. By childhood, the spleen shrivels into a tiny calcified fibrous knob, a process called autosplenectomy. Without a functioning spleen, patients lose antibody protection against encapsulated bacteria, placing them at immense risk of fatal pneumococcal sepsis and Salmonella bone infections.

vis.title: Splenic Pathology in Sickle Cell Disease
rows: Loss of IgM memory B cell opsonization
Total fibrotic obliteration of red pulp
Howell-Jolly bodies on peripheral blood smear

steps.tx: Definitive diagnosis requires alkaline and acidic **haemoglobin electrophoresis** or high-performance liquid chromatography. In homozygous sickle cell disease (HbSS), hemoglobin S accounts for eighty-five to ninety-five percent of total hemoglobin, hemoglobin F comprises five to fifteen percent, and normal adult hemoglobin A is completely absent. In benign heterozygous sickle cell trait (HbAS), hemoglobin A predominates at sixty percent, protecting against severe sickling.
steps.say: Confirm the diagnosis with hemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC. In homozygous sickle cell disease, hemoglobin S dominates at eighty-five to ninety-five percent, with elevated fetal hemoglobin, and hemoglobin A is completely absent. In benign sickle cell trait, normal hemoglobin A makes up sixty percent, preventing sickling except under extreme hypoxia.

left.title: Sickle Cell Disease (HbSS)
points: HbS: 85 to 95 percent of total hemoglobin

right.title: Sickle Cell Trait (HbAS)
points: HbS: 35 to 40 percent of total hemoglobin

quiz.q: What specific amino acid substitution causes the formation of hemoglobin S?
options: Valine replaces glutamic acid at codon 6 of the beta-globin chain
Lysine replaces glutamic acid at codon 6 of the beta-globin chain
Glutamic acid replaces valine at codon 26 of the alpha-globin chain
Arginine replaces histidine at codon 146 of the beta-globin chain
quiz.explain: A point mutation (GAG to GTG) at codon 6 of the beta-globin gene substitutes non-polar valine for negatively charged glutamic acid, creating HbS.

quiz.q: What peripheral blood smear finding indicates functional asplenia following autosplenectomy in sickle cell anaemia?
quiz.explain: Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear DNA remnants normally pitted out by the spleen) persist in circulating red cells following autosplenectomy.
